summary:
Walking uphill must eventually reach a summit, because the trail ends in a drop on both sides. So at `mid`,
if the next point is higher, a summit exists to the right; otherwise one exists at mid or to its left.
Binary search keeps the half that's guaranteed to contain a summit: O(log n). Any summit is accepted.

question.md:
Heights have no equal neighbours; the trail drops to −∞ before the first and after the last point. Return the
index of **any** point higher than both neighbours, in O(log n).

- **Any summit** is accepted; there may be several.
- **The ends can be summits** thanks to the imaginary drops: `[7]` → 0; `[1, 2]` → 1.
- **Heights span the full 32-bit range**, but only comparisons are needed, so no overflow risk.
- **The input isn't sorted**, yet binary search still works.

think.md:
Take `[2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 8, 6, 7, 0]`. Summits are at indices [1, 5, 7]. We only need one.

Stand at any point and look right. If the next point is **higher**, keep walking right while it keeps rising.
You can't climb forever: either the trail turns down (that's a summit) or it ends (the last point, with a
drop after it, is a summit). So **"the next point is higher" guarantees a summit to the right**. Likewise, if
the next point is lower, a summit exists at the current point or to its left.

think.caption: Any of the shaded points is a valid answer.

think.md:
That's enough for binary search. At mid: rising to the right → `lo = mid + 1`; falling → `hi = mid`. The kept
half always contains a summit, and when one index is left, it is one.

approaches.title: Scan for the first downturn

idea.md: Return the first index i whose next point is lower, or the last index if the trail never turns down. Every point before i was rising, so i is higher than its left neighbour too.

build: For i from 0 to n − 2: if `h[i] > h[i + 1]`, return i.

lines.text: The first point higher than the next. It was reached by climbing (or is index 0, with a drop before it), so it beats its left neighbour as well.
Climbing all the way: the last point is a summit thanks to the drop after it.

steps.text: 5 > 3: since we got here by climbing, it's higher than both neighbours. Summit at 1.

walk.title: Scan for the first point that is higher than the point after it (or the last point).

limits.md: Linear; the requirement is O(log n). The "walk uphill" argument works from any midpoint, not just from the start.

approaches.title: Binary search uphill

idea.md: `lo = 0`, `hi = n − 1`. If `h[mid] < h[mid + 1]`, a summit lies right: `lo = mid + 1`. Else one lies at mid or left: `hi = mid`. Return `lo`.

build: Compare mid with mid + 1; keep the uphill half.

lines.text: A summit exists somewhere in the whole trail.
Go towards the higher neighbour: a summit is guaranteed that way. Invariant: `[lo, hi]` always contains a summit.
One index left: it's a summit.

steps.text: lo=0, hi=8, mid=4: 4 < 8, so the trail rises after mid: a summit lies to the right, lo = 5.
lo=5, hi=8, mid=6: 6 < 7, so the trail rises after mid: a summit lies to the right, lo = 7.
lo=7, hi=8, mid=7: 7 > 0, so the trail falls after mid: a summit lies at mid or to its left, hi = 7.
lo = hi = 7: 7 is higher than its neighbours.

walk.title: Compare mid with its right neighbour and walk uphill: there is always a summit in the uphill direction.

takeaways.md:
- **Peak finding:** move towards the higher neighbour; the boundary drops guarantee a peak in that
  direction, so binary search works on unsorted data.
- The invariant "the range contains a valid answer" is what makes it correct, not sortedness.
